Sub: Notice of the 29th Annual General Meeting and Annual Report for the Financial Year 2025-26. 
 
Dear Sir/ Madam, 
Pursuant to Regulations 30 and 34 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 ( “Listing Regulations” ), we hereby inform that the 29th 
Annual General Meeting (“AGM”)  of the Members of the Company is scheduled to be held on 
Wednesday, September 30, 2026  at 12:30 p.m.  ("IST") through Video Conferencing/ Other Audio 
Visual Means ("VC/ OAVM") in compliance with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, 
rules framed thereunder, Listing Regulations and circulars issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs 
(“MCA”) and Securities and Exchange Board of India ( “SEBI”) (collectively referred to as “ Circulars” ) 
in this regard.   
 
In accordance with the aforesaid circulars, the Notice of AGM and Annual Report of the Company for the 
Financial Year 2025-26 is being sent through electronic mode to all those members of the Company whose 
email addresses are registered with the Company / Company’s Registrar and Share Transfer Agent or 
Depositories/ Depository Participants. 
 
Further, in compliance with Regulation 36(1)(b) of the Listing Regulations, a letter is being sent to 
Members whose e-mail id are not registered with the Company/the Registrar and  Share Transfer Agent/the 
Depository Participant(s), providing the exact weblink where the Annual Report for the Financial Year 
2025-26 and the Notice of the 29th AGM can be accessed on the Company’s website. 
 
The Members, holding shares as on the cut-off date i.e. Wednesday, September 23, 2026  will be entitled 
to avail the facility of remote e-voting as well as voting at the AGM on the Resolutions set forth in the 
Notice of AGM. 
 
The remote e-Voting facility would be available during the following period: 
 
Commencement of Remote e-Voting 09:00 a.m. (IST) on Saturday, September 26, 2026  
End of Remote e-Voting 05:00 p.m. (IST) on Tuesday, September 29, 2026

Step 1: Access through Depositories CDSL / NSDL e-Voting 
system in case of individual shareholders holding shares in 
demat mode.

(i) The voting period begins at 09:00 a.m. (IST) on Saturday, 
September 26, 2026 and ends at 05:00 p.m. (IST) 
on Tuesday, September 29, 2026. During this period 
shareholders’ of the Company, as on the cut-off date i.e. 
Wednesday, September 23, 2026 may cast their vote 
electronically. The e-voting module shall be disabled by 
CDSL for voting thereafter.
(ii) Shareholders who have already voted prior to the meeting 
date would not be entitled to vote at the meeting.
(iii) Pursuant to SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD/ 
CIR/P/2020/242 dated December 09, 2020, under 
Regulation 44 of Listing Regulations, listed entities are required to provide remote e-voting facility to its 
shareholders, in respect of all shareholders’ resolutions. 
However, it has been observed that the participation by the 
public non-institutional shareholders / retail shareholders 
is at a negligible level. Currently, there are multiple e-voting 
service providers (ESPs) providing e-voting facility to 
listed entities in India. This necessitates registration on 
various ESPs and maintenance of multiple user IDs and 
passwords by the shareholders.
(iv) In order to increase the efficiency of the voting process, 
pursuant to a public consultation, it has been decided to 
enable e-voting to all the demat account holders, by way 
of a single login credential, through their demat accounts/ 
websites of Depositories/ Depository Participants. Demat 
account holders would be able to cast their vote without 
having to register again with the ESPs, thereby, not only 
facilitating seamless authentication but also enhancing 
ease and convenience of participating in e-voting process.
Step 1: Access through Depositories CDSL / NSDL e-Voting 
system in case of individual shareholders holding shares in 
demat mode.
(v) In terms of SEBI circular no. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD/ 
CIR/P/2020/242 dated December 9, 2020 on e-Voting 
facility provided by Listed Companies, Individual 
shareholders holding securities in demat mode are allowed 
to vote through their demat account maintained with 
Depositories and Depository Participants. Shareholders

(Pursuant to Section 102 of the Companies Act, 2013)
The relevant Explanatory Statement pursuant to Section 102 of the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act ”), as amended from time to

Item No. 3
The Articles of Association (“ AoA ”) of the Company presently contain specific rights and references pertaining to Late  
Mr. Rakesh Jhunjhunwala (“RJ”). Given that RJ no longer holds Equity Shares of the Company pursuant to the Shareholders 
Agreement dated May 18, 2004, and to align the AoA with the current governance framework of the Company, it is proposed to 
alter the AoA by deleting all references to RJ, wherever appearing therein, and omitting the relevant provisions relating to the rights 
and entitlements associated with him.
The Board at its meeting held on August 06, 2026 has approved to alter the AoA of the Company by deleting all the references of 
RJ in the following Article(s) which shall be omitted, subject to the approval of the members of the Company:
	 Section A and C of Part II;
	 In Article 175.1(d) the words “other than the rights granted to Mr. Rakesh Jhunjhunwala under shareholders agreement dated 
May 18, 2004” stand deleted; and 
 Post deletion of the above Sections, subsequent Articles will be renumbered accordingly.
Accordingly, the Board recommends the Special Resolution as set out in Item No. 3 of the Notice for approval of the members to 
alter the AoA by deleting the above mentioned Articles. 
The copy of the draft of the amended AOA will be available for inspection at the registered office and corporate office of the 
Company during normal business hours on all working days of the Company (except Saturdays and Sundays) and shall also be made 
available for inspection through other modes in accordance with applicable laws.
None of the Directors, Key Managerial Personnel of the Company or their respective relatives is concerned or interested, financially 
or otherwise, in the proposed resolution, except to the extent of their shareholding, if any, in the Company.
Item No. 4
As part of internal restructuring of group companies, DNEG S.a.r.l., a material subsidiary of the Company (“DNEG” or “Seller”) 
proposes to sell entire shareholding (including as currently held and the remaining shareholding which shall be acquired from 
other shareholders) in Brahma AI Services India Limited (formerly known as Prime Focus T echnologies Limited), (“Brahma India”) 
to Brahma AI Holdings Limited (“Brahma” or “Purchaser”), a material step down subsidiary of Prime Focus Limited (“PFL” / “the 
Company”), for a consideration amount of upto USD 90.09 Million on terms and conditions as set forth in the Share Purchase 
Agreement (“SPA ”) entered into by DNEG and Brahma (“Proposed Sale”), subject to shareholders’ approval and other consents / 
approvals as may be required.
The Proposed Sale was approved by the Audit Committee and Board of Directors of the Company at their meeting(s) held on  
April 01, 2026.
In terms of the provisions of Regulation 23(4) and Regulation 24(6) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations 2015, as amended (the “Listing Regulations”), the consent of the Members 
would be required in accordance with the provisions thereof, for the Proposed Sale.
In terms of Regulation 23(4) of Listing Regulations, the Proposed Sale would be considered a material related party transaction 
and as per provisions of Regulation 24(6) of the Listing Regulations, it shall result in disposal of entire existing shares held by the 
DNEG in Brahma India resulting in selling of assets amounting to more than twenty percent of the assets of the material subsidiary. 
Accordingly, shareholders’ approval by way of (i) ordinary resolution will be required pursuant to Regulation 23(4) of the Listing 
Regulations and (ii) special resolution will be required pursuant to Regulation 24(6) of the Listing Regulations. Accordingly, the 
approval is being obtained from the shareholders and will be subject to the requirements of the abovementioned provisions.
As per Regulation 23(4) of the Listing Regulations, no related party shall vote to approve resolutions for material related party 
transactions whether the entity is a related party to the particular transaction or not, and accordingly, the related parties of the 
Company in accordance with Listing Regulations, shall not vote for the Proposed Sale.
The Audit Committee has reviewed the certificate confirming that the terms of related party transaction (“RPT”) proposed to 
be entered into are in the interest of the Listed Entity i.e. Prime Focus Limited given by Whole Time Director namely Mr. Naresh 
Mahendranath Malhotra and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) namely Mr. Vikas Rathee of the Company.

Item No. 6
In terms of Regulation 17(6)(a) of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”), as amended from time to time, the payment of any fees or compensation to Non-
Executive Directors (including Independent Directors) requires approval of shareholders in general meeting. 
The members are further informed that, where a company has no profits or inadequate profits, Section 149(9) and Section 197(3) 
of the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act ”) permit payment of remuneration to the Non-Executive Directors (including Independent 
Directors) exclusive of any fees payable under Section 197(5) of the Act in accordance with Schedule V to the Act. Proviso under 
Part II, Section II of Schedule V to the Act prescribes limits for remuneration payable to “other directors” (which term means non-
executive directors and independent directors) and permits payment of remuneration in excess of limits provided in the T able 
therein, where the Members approve the same by way of a special resolution, subject to compliance with the conditions set out 
therein.
It is pertinent to note here that the Non-Executive Directors including the Independent Directors of the Company devote their 
valuable time, bring with them significant professional expertise and rich experience across a wide spectrum of functional areas 
giving critical advice to the Company and accordingly they should be appropriately compensated for the same both in case of 
inadequacy of profits or losses. 
In view of the above, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee of the Company (“NRC”) and the Board of Directors of the 
Company (“Board”) at their respective meetings both held on May 28, 2026 have considered and recommended payment of 
remuneration to the Non-Executive Directors, including Independent Directors, of the Company, subject to approval of the 
members by way of a special resolution and such other approvals, consents or permissions as may be required under applicable law. 
Considering the size and complexity of the Company’s business, the time commitment expected from the Non-Executive Directors, 
including Independent Directors, their committee responsibilities, experience, expertise and contribution to Board deliberations, it 
is proposed that remuneration of up to ` 2,00,00,000/- (Rupees Two Crore only) per annum be paid to each Non-Executive Director, 
including each Independent Director, for a period of three financial years commencing from April 1, 2026 and ending on March 31, 
2029 (the “Remuneration”).

Item no. 8 to 15 
Regulation 23 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing Regulations’), as amended 
from time to time, effective April 01, 2022, states that all material related party shall require prior approval of Members by means 
of an Ordinary Resolution as per limit specified in Listing Regulations. The said limits are applicable, even if the transactions are 
in the ordinary course of business of the concerned company and at arm’s length basis. The amended Regulation 2(1)(zc) of the 
Listing Regulations has also expanded the definition of related party transaction which now includes within its ambit a transaction 
involving a transfer of resources, services or obligations between (i) a listed entity or any of its subsidiaries on one hand and a 
related party of the listed entity or any of its subsidiaries on the other hand or (ii) a listed entity or any of its subsidiaries on one 
hand, and any other person or entity on the other hand, the purpose and effect of which is to benefit a related party of the listed 
entity or any of its subsidiaries, regardless of whether a price is charged or not.
=== page 33 ===
31Further, in case of omnibus approval for material related party transactions is obtained from the shareholders in mode other than 
AGM, validity of such omnibus approvals shall not exceed one year and if approved in an AGM shall be valid upto the date of the 
next AGM as per the provisions of Companies Act, 2013. Accordingly, the said resolutions are being presented for the approval of 
shareholders, so as to extend the validity of shareholders’ approval for this resolution until the next Annual General Meeting of the 
Company to be held in FY 2027-28.
The Management has provided the Audit Committee with relevant details of the proposed RPT s, including material terms and basis 
of pricing, if any. The Audit Committee, after reviewing all necessary information, has granted its approval for entering into the 
below mentioned RPT s, subject to approval by the Members at the Annual General Meeting. The Audit Committee has noted that 
the said transaction(s) will be at an arm’s length pricing basis and will be in the ordinary course of business.
The Company /Subsidaries of the Company now proposes to enter into related party transactions as provided in resolutions at 
Item Nos. 8 to 15, during FY 2026-27 and FY 2027-28, at the agreed terms of the transactions. Accordingly, the approval of the 
shareholders is being sought for the resolutions contained at Item Nos. 8 to 15 of the accompanying Notice.
The Members may note that in terms of the provisions of the Listing Regulations, the related parties as defined thereunder (whether 
such related party(ies) is a party to the aforesaid transactions or not), shall not vote to approve the said resolutions.

109Item No. 16:
The present authorised share capital of the Company is ` 85,00,00,000 (Rupees Eighty-Five Crore Only) divided into 85,00,00,000 
(Eighty-Five Crore) equity shares of the Company having a face value of Re. 1/- (Rupee One Only) each (“Equity Shares”).
In view of the present size of the Company’s operations and in order to support future capital-raising initiatives and meet the 
Company’s anticipated financial and operational needs, additional funds are required by the Company. Therefore, it is proposed 
to increase the authorised share capital of the Company from ` 85,00,00,000 (Rupees Eighty-Five Crore Only) divided into 
85,00,00,000 (Eighty-Five Crore) Equity Shares of Re. 1/- (Rupee One Only) each to ` 1,00,00,00,000/- (Rupees One Hundred 
Crore Only) divided into 1,00,00,00,000 (One Hundred Crore) Equity Shares of Re. 1/- (Rupee One Only) each ranking pari-passu in 
all respects with the existing Equity Shares of the Company.
Consequently, Clause ‘V’ of the Memorandum of Association of the Company would also require alteration so as to reflect the 
changed authorized share capital of the Company. Accordingly, the necessary amendment in the Memorandum of Association of 
the Company is proposed in order to reflect the enhanced authorised share capital of the Company.
As per the provisions of Section 61 of the Companies Act, 2013, as amended from time to time, along with the relevant rules and 
regulations made thereunder (“Act ”), an increase in the authorised share capital of a company and consequential alteration of 
Clause ‘V’ of its memorandum of association, approval of the members of the company is required by way of an Ordinary Resolution.
The Board of Directors of the Company accordingly recommends the resolution as set out at Item No. 16 of the accompanying 
Notice for the approval of the Members as an Ordinary Resolution. A copy of the Memorandum of Association of the Company duly 
amended is available for inspection through electronic mode upto the date of Annual General Meeting.
None of the Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of the Company or their respective relatives are, in any way, concerned or 
interested, financially or otherwise, in the proposed resolution, except to the extent of their shareholding, if any, in the Company.
Item No. 17:
The Company is evaluating various opportunities to strengthen its balance sheet, optimise its capital structure and improve its 
financial flexibility. In this regard, the Company proposes to evaluate and, subject to receipt of applicable approvals, undertake a 
capital-raising exercise for an amount not exceeding ` 3,000 Crore (Rupees Three Thousand Crore Only) or its equivalent in any 
other currency, in one or more tranches, and through one or more permissible instruments or modes.
At this stage, the Company has not finalised the specific instrument or structure for the proposed capital raise. The proposed 
capital raise may, inter alia, comprise equity shares and/or other eligible securities, including warrants and/or other equity-linked 
securities, whether convertible or non-convertible, through permissible modes including private placement, Qualified Institutions 
Placement (QIP), issuance of Depository Receipts (ADR/GDR), preferential issue, rights issue or any other permissible method or 
combination thereof, subject to applicable laws and regulatory requirements.
The final size, timing, instrument, mode and structure of the proposed capital raise shall be determined subsequently by the Board 
of Directors of the Company after evaluating the available alternatives and prevailing market conditions.
The primary proposed utilisation of the proceeds of the proposed fund raise would be towards repayment and/or prepayment 
of existing indebtedness of the Company and/or its subsidiaries. The balance, if any, may be utilised towards transaction-related 
expenses, general corporate purposes including growth capital and/or such other purposes as may be permissible under applicable 
laws including the Companies Act, 2013 (“Act ”) and as approved by the appropriate authority.
The proposed fund raising is intended primarily to reduce indebtedness and finance costs of the Company and/or its subsidiaries, 
strengthen the balance sheet, optimise the capital structure, improve financial flexibility and create greater headroom to support 
the Company’s future strategic and growth initiatives.
The proposed fund raising shall be undertaken in compliance with the applicable laws, including the applicable provisions of the Act, 
the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, as amended (“SEBI 
ICDR Regulations”), the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 
2015, as amended (“SEBI Listing Regulations”), and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, as amended.
In terms of Section 62(1)(c) of the Act provides, inter alia, that when it is proposed to increase the issued capital of a company by 
allotment of further equity shares, to any persons other than the existing members of the company, such issuance shall be subject 
to a special resolution. Since the special resolution proposed may result in the issuance of equity shares of the Company to persons 
other than existing members of the Company, approval of the members of the Company is being sought pursuant to the provisions 
of Section 62(1)(c) and other applicable provisions of the Act as well as applicable rules notified by the Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs and in terms of the provisions of SEBI ICDR Regulations.
Further, as per Rule 14(1) of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, a company can make a private 
placement of its securities under the Act only after receipt of prior approval of its members by way of a Special Resolution. Consent 
of the members would therefore be necessary pursuant to the aforementioned provisions of the Act read with applicable provisions 
=== page 112 ===
110of the SEBI ICDR Regulations and the SEBI Listing Regulations, for issuance of securities.
Accordingly, the approval of the members of the Company is sought by way of a Special Resolution to enable the Company to 
evaluate and undertake the proposed capital raise of up to ` 3,000 Crore (Rupees Three Thousand Crore Only) or its equivalent 
in any other currency in one or more tranches, and through one or more permissible instruments/modes, and to undertake all such 
acts, deeds, matters and things as may be necessary or incidental in connection therewith, subject to applicable laws and corporate 
and regulatory approvals.
The Board of Directors, at its meeting held on September 4, 2026, considered and approved the proposal and recommends the 
resolution as set out at Item No. 17 of the accompanying Notice for approval by the Members as a Special Resolution.
None of the Directors, Key Managerial Personnel of the Company or their respective relatives are, in any way, concerned or 
interested, financially or otherwise, in the proposed resolution, except to the extent of their respective shareholding, if any, in the 
Company.
The relevant documents, if any, in connection with the proposed resolution shall be available for inspection by the members in 
accordance with the applicable provisions of the Act.

12. RISK MANAGEMENT
 The Company is exposed to inherent uncertainties owing to the 
sectors in which it operates. A key factor in determining a Company’s 
capacity to create sustainable value is the risk that the Company is 
willing to take (at strategic and operational levels) and its ability to 
manage them effectively. Many risks exist in a Company’s operating 
environment and they emerge on a regular basis. The Company’s 
Risk Management processes focuses on ensuring that these risks 
are identified on a timely basis and addressed. The Board has a duly 
constituted Risk Management Committee of Directors.
 The Company is well aware of the above risks and as a part of 
business strategy has a robust risk management framework to 
identify, evaluate and mitigate business risks with timely action. 
This framework seeks to enable growth, create transparency, 
minimize adverse impact on the business objectives and enhance 
the Company’s competitive advantage by undertaking effective 
steps to manage risks.
 The Board approved Risk Management Policy has been put in place, 
which is reviewed periodically, to establish appropriate system and 
procedures to mitigate all risks faced by the Company.
 The Risk Management policy of the Company is available on 
the website at https://www.primefocus.com/wp-content/
uploads/2025/04/Risk_Management_Policy.pdf

to strengthening of the Company’s risk management policies and

15. PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT
 The Company has zero tolerance for sexual harassment at 
workplace and has a mechanism in place for prevention, prohibition 
and redressal of sexual harassment at workplace in line with the 
provisions of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace 
(Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 and the Rules 
made thereunder. The Company is committed to provide equal 
opportunities without regard to their race, caste, sex, religion, 
color, nationality, disability, etc. All employees are treated with 
dignity with a view to maintain a work environment free of 
sexual harassment whether physical, verbal or psychological. All 
employees (permanent, contractual, temporary and trainees) are 
covered.
 The Company has in place an Anti-Sexual Harassment Policy in 
line with the requirements of the Sexual Harassment of Women at 
Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition & Redressal) Act, 2013.
 An Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) has been set up to redress 
complaints received regarding sexual harassment at workplace.

27 . BOARD EVALUATION
 Pursuant to the provisions of the Act and the corporate governance 
requirements as prescribed by the Listing Regulations, annual 
evaluation of the performance of the Board, its Committees and of 
individual Directors has been made.
 The performance evaluation of the Independent Directors was 
carried out by the entire Board, excluding the Director being 
evaluated. The performance evaluation of the Chairman and the 
Non Independent Directors were carried out by the Independent 
Directors who also reviewed the performance of the Board as a 
whole. The Nomination and Remuneration Committee also reviewed 
the performance of the Board, its Committees and of the Directors.
 The criteria for performance evaluation of the Board included 
aspects like Board composition and structure, effectiveness of 
Board processes, information and functioning, etc. The criteria 
for performance evaluation of Committees of the Board included 
aspects like composition of Committees, effectiveness of 
Committee meetings, etc. The criteria for performance evaluation 
of the individual Directors included aspects on contribution to the 
Board and Committee meetings, preparedness on the issues to be 
discussed, meaningful and constructive contribution and inputs in 
meetings, etc. In addition, the Chairperson was also evaluated on 
the key aspects of his role. The criteria for performance evaluation 
of Independent Directors included aspects like time invested in  
understanding the company and its unique requirements; External 
knowledge and perspective brought to the table for discussion at 
the meetings; Expresses his / her views on the issues discussed at 
the meeting; and keeps himself/herself updated with the area and 
issue that are likely to be discussed at the Board level. Criteria for Determining Qualifications, Positive Attributes and 
Independence of a Director
 In terms of the provisions of Section 178(3) of the Act and 
Regulation 19 of the Listing Regulations, the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee (NRC) has formulated the criteria for 
determining qualifications, positive attributes and independence 
of Directors, the key features of which are as follows:
• Qualifications –  The Board nomination process encourages 
diversity of thought, experience, knowledge, age and gender. 
It also ensures that the Board has an appropriate blend of 
functional and industry expertise.
• Positive Attributes -  Apart from the duties of Directors 
as prescribed in the Act, the Directors are expected 
to demonstrate high standards of ethical behavior, 
communication skills and independent judgment. The 
Directors are also expected to abide by the respective Code 
of Conduct as applicable to them.
• Independence - A Director will be considered independent if 
he/ she meets the criteria laid down in Section 149(6) of the 
Act, the Rules framed thereunder and Regulation 16(1)(b) of 
the Listing Regulations.

43. INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY
 The Company acquired the Film and Media Services business 
(“FMS” ) from Reliance MediaWorks Limited  ( “RMW” ) in July 2014, 
by way of a Business Transfer Agreement dated November 19, 
2014, for a total  consideration of ` 55,000.00 Lakhs, of which the 
Company paid a consideration of ` 35,000.00 Lakhs to RMW by 
way of an allotment of equity shares of a commensurate value on 
April 7 ,2015. The remaining consideration of ` 20,000.00 Lakhs 
was structured as debt to be paid by the Company to Reliance Alpha 
Services Private Limited, now known as Raspalfa Services Private 
Limited ( ‘ R A S P L” ), over the course of a few years under a Loan 
Agreement dated February 25, 2019. 
 On August 29, 2023, the Company received a notice that a petition 
had been filed before the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai 
Bench ( “NCLT” ), Mumbai by RASPL to initiate corporate insolvency 
resolution process under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 
2016 ( “IBC” ) with respect to alleged breach / default under the 
Loan Agreement dated February 25, 2019, by the Company and 
claiming a sum of ` 35,379.75 Lakhs. By a pronouncement dated 
May 06, 2026, the NCLT pronounced admission of the petition 
filed by RASPL under Section 7 of the IBC against the Company. 
Immediately upon the pronouncement, appropriate appellate 
proceedings were initiated before the Hon’ble National Company 
Law Appellate Tribunal ( “NCLAT” ), seeking urgent relief, including 
stay of operation of the said order. 
 On May 12, 2026, the NCLAT stayed the NCLT order dated May 06, 
2026, directed that the Interim Resolution Professional shall not 
take any further steps in pursuance of the said order, and directed 
deposit of ` 35,379.75 Lakhs in an interest-bearing account with 
the Registrar, NCLAT, by May 20, 2026. The said deposit direction 
has been complied with before the due date by way of creation of a 
fixed deposit for the said amount and marking of lien in favour of the 
Registrar, NCLAT. 
 RASPL disputed the mode of compliance and filed I.A. No. 3835 
of 2026 before the NCLAT seeking vacation of the interim order 
dated May 12, 2026. RASPL also filed Civil Appeal No. 7946 of 
2026 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court challenging the NCLAT 
interim order dated May 12, 2026. By order dated May 25, 
2026, the Hon’ble Supreme Court disposed off the civil appeal 
=== page 160 ===
Prime Focus Limited 42without interfering with the NCLAT interim order, observing that 
interference at this stage was not required and that the parties may 
raise all contentions before the NCLAT. Thereafter, I.A. No. 3835 of 
2026 was listed before the NCLAT on May 27 , 2026. The NCLAT 
recorded the submission regarding the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
order dated May 25, 2026 and dismissed I.A. No. 3835 of 2026 as 
not being pressed in view of the said Hon’ble Supreme Court order. 
The main appeal is listed on July 9, 2026 for further hearing. The 
matter is currently sub judice and under consideration before the 
NCL AT. 
 The Company has made appropriate accruals in the books of account 
as at March 31, 2026, and based on professional legal advice, 
management believes that no additional material adjustment is 
required to the financial statements at this stage. The Company has 
adequate financial resources in place to meet any obligation that 
may ultimately be determined upon settiement or adjudication of 
the above matter.

Prime Focus Limited 56Management Discussion & Analysis
Section I. Company Profile 
Company background
Prime Focus Limited (along with its subsidiaries hereafter referred to as 
“PFL ” or the “Company”), established in 1997, has evolved into a leading 
global provider of end-to-end post-production and media services. The 
Company offers a comprehensive range of creative and technology-driven 
solutions, including visual effects (VFX), stereo 3D conversion, animation, 
technology products and services, production equipment rental, 
soundstages, digital intermediate and picture post-production services. 
Through its integrated service offerings, PFL enables storytellers and 
content creators to focus on their creative vision while efficiently 
managing complex production requirements that involve advanced 
technology, skilled talent and critical resources.
PFL ’s subsidiaries, Brahma AI Services India Limited (“Brahma India”) and 
DNEG S.A.R.L. (“DNEG”), play a significant role in delivering advanced 
creative, technology and production services globally. The acquisition of 
DNEG in 2014 marked a transformational milestone for the Company, 
significantly strengthening its position in the global visual effects and 
animation industry. DNEG has since earned multiple prestigious industry 
awards and recognition for delivering exceptional Visual Effects (VFX) 
work across globally acclaimed projects. The subsidiary continues to 
expand its international footprint, reflecting its position as a leading 
global media and entertainment company. The Company, along with its 
group entities, employs over 10,200 professionals across 24 locations 
globally. PFL serves a diversified and distinguished client base comprising 
leading Hollywood studios, Over-the-T op (OTT) platforms, broadcasters, 
advertisers and production houses. The Company collaborates closely 
with content creators to deliver high-quality output, operational efficiency 
and cost optimisation. A substantial portion of the Company’s revenues is 
derived from Hollywood studios. 
During FY 2025-26, the Company further expanded its presence 
in immersive entertainment by delivering screen-based content for 
Universal’s Harry Potter theme park rides and advancing the development 
of two full-length digital concerts, strengthening its capabilities in next-
generation digital entertainment experiences.
During the year, the Company further advanced its strategic focus on 
Artificial Intelligence and next-generation digital technologies. BRAHMA, 
DNEG’s integrated AI platform, acquired Metaphysic, a pioneer in 
generative AI technologies. BRAHMA is integrating DNEG’s award-winning 
VFX capabilities; Ziva’s advanced digital human technologies, Metaphysic’s 
AI-powered neural performance tools and CLEAR®’s AI-driven platform to 
develop a comprehensive suite of innovative solutions. These technologies 
are expected to significantly enhance the creation of realistic AI-powered 
digital humans and unlock opportunities across diverse sectors, including 
entertainment, healthcare, education and immersive digital experiences.During the year, the Company further strengthened its strategic focus 
on Artificial Intelligence and next-generation content technologies 
by evolving BRAHMA AI into a unified enterprise AI platform. Built by 
integrating Brahma India’s CLEAR® platform with Metaphysic’s advanced 
AI capabilities, BRAHMA AI’s platform combines AI-driven content 
workflows, digital humans, multilingual localisation and intelligent content 
orchestration within a secure enterprise ecosystem.
BRAHMA AI is developing innovative solutions designed to transform 
content creation, management and distribution at scale. Built on its Mind² 
philosophy, it combines human creativity with AI-driven scale to enable 
faster workflows, smarter decisions and global content delivery. These 
capabilities are unlocking significant opportunities across industries, 
including media & entertainment, healthcare, brands & agencies, 
enterprise communications, education and retail.
Section 2 - Economic Overview
Global Economy
The global economy continued to navigate a dynamic, interconnected 
environment during the year, shaped by evolving structural trends, policy 
changes and persistent geopolitical tensions. Ongoing conflicts in West 
Asia disrupted global supply chains and contributed to volatility in crude 
oil and energy prices, while tariff measures and trade policy actions by the 
United States further pressured global trade flows, manufacturing activity 
and cross-border investments. Despite these challenges, the global 
economy remained resilient, aided by the growing adoption of Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) across industries, which improved business efficiency and 
workflows, as well as by steady consumer demand and a gradual recovery 
in overall economic activity. Global growth remained stable at around 
3.4% in both 2024 and 2025 and is projected to moderate slightly to 
3.1% in 2026, then improve marginally to 3.2% in 2027.
The United States grew by 2.1% in 2025, driven by strong investments 
in the technology sector and supportive financial conditions, even as 
inflation stayed elevated and labour market momentum weakened. The 
Euro Area posted modest but steadily improving growth of 1.4% in 2025, 
up from 0.9% in 2024, as inflation moved closer to target levels and 
the region adjusted to prior energy shocks and to tight monetary policy. 
China continued to record relatively strong economic growth during 
the year, driven mainly by exports, while domestic demand remained 
uneven, particularly in the real estate sector. Meanwhile, Southeast Asian 
economies witnessed healthy growth, driven by strong technology exports 
and ongoing supply chain diversification, although the region remains 
exposed to external challenges, including fluctuations in global energy 
prices.

Outlook
Despite geopolitical tensions and occasional disruptions in energy and 
trade markets, the global economy is projected to remain largely stable. 
In the longer run, structural drivers such as demographic changes, evolving 
consumer preferences and better access to markets and services are 
expected to underpin growth. Sustained expansion will rely on continued 
adoption of new technologies and stronger coordination across global 
policy frameworks. Among major economies, the United States is likely 
to stay driven by resilient demand and investment activity, while the Euro 
Area is expected to experience a gradual recovery. China is stabilising as it 
undergoes structural adjustments, aided by policy support and Southeast 
Asia continues to gain from strong manufacturing activity, export 
momentum and steady domestic consumption.

Indian Economy
India continues to remain one of the fastest-growing major economies 
globally, accelerated by strong domestic consumption, a large young 
workforce, ongoing infrastructure development and sustained policy 
reforms. The Indian economy demonstrated resilience during FY 2025–26, 
with GDP growth improving to 7.6% compared to 7.1% in FY 2024–25, 
according to revised estimates released by the Ministry of Statistics and 
Programme Implementation (MoSPI) based on the 2022–23 base year. 
Strong consumer demand, rising urbanisation and continued government 
focus on capital expenditure supported economic activity across key 
sectors. India’s services sector remained a key growth driver, supported by 
increasing global demand for digital transformation, cloud-based 
technologies and AI-led services. The country’s strong talent base, growing 
digital ecosystem and leadership in global outsourcing continued to drive 
expansion in technology and business services exports.

India’s long-term economic outlook remains positive, accelerated by a

Section 3. Industry Overview
Global Media & Entertainment (M&E) Industry 
The global M&E industry continues to expand as digital adoption, 
advertising, artificial intelligence (AI), streaming and demand for live 
experiences reshape the sector. According to PwC’s Global Entertainment 
& Media Outlook 2026–30, global M&E revenues from advertising, 
=== page 176 ===
Prime Focus Limited 58connectivity and consumer spending reached US$ 3.5 trillion in 2025, 
registering 5.3% growth over the previous year. The global M&E industry 
is expected to grow at a CAGR of 3.4% between 2025 and 2030, reaching 
US$ 4.2 trillion by 2030. The global M&E industry expansion is expected 
to generate around US$ 600 billion in additional annual revenue by 2030, 
with digital ecosystems accounting for a significant share of this growth.
Global M&E Industry Revenue (US$  trillion)
Source: PwC Global M&E In dustry Report (2026-2030)
The global M&E industry is undergoing a structural shift as increasingly 
powerful digital technologies, particularly AI, change how content is 
created, distributed, discovered and monetised. While digital platforms 
continue to shape consumption patterns, consumer demand for human 
connection remains strong. Live sports, concerts, cinema, trade shows 
and other immersive experiences are expected to gain importance as 
consumers seek more social, emotional and real-world interactions 
alongside digital entertainment.
Advertising is expected to remain the fastest-growing of the three major 
M&E revenue categories. Global advertising expenditure surpassed US$ 
1.1 trillion in 2025 and is projected to reach US$ 1.4 trillion by 2030, 
representing a 5.6% CAGR. Advertising is expected to overtake consumer 
spending as the largest growth category in 2026, supported by increasing 
digital consumption, improved targeting and AI-enabled personalisation. 
Within advertising, internet advertising remains a major growth area. 
Global internet advertising revenue increased 12.2% Y oY to US$ 755.6 
billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at a 7.2% CAGR through 2030. 
Retail media, social media, online video and other digital formats are 
gaining share as brands seek measurable engagement and closer links 
between advertising and purchasing decisions. AI is also changing digital 
advertising by enabling more precise targeting, real-time personalisation 
and improved campaign optimisation. This is expected to support higher-
value advertising formats, including connected TV and shoppable video.
Streaming remains an important growth segment, although its expansion 
is expected to moderate as mature markets experience increasing 
subscription fatigue. Global over-the-top (OTT) revenues increased 13.9% 
in 2025 to US$ 226.6 billion and are projected to reach US$ 304 billion by 
2030, representing a 6.1% CAGR.As consumers become more selective about the number of subscriptions 
they maintain, streaming platforms are increasingly adopting advertising-
supported tiers, bundled offerings and partnerships to improve 
monetisation and reduce churn. OTT advertising currently accounts for 
19.4% of OTT revenues and is projected to grow at a 9.4% CAGR, reaching 
22.6% of segment revenues by 2030. At the same time, traditional 
television continues to face structural pressure from digital alternatives. 
Global traditional TV revenues declined 2.7% in 2025 to US$ 360.5 billion 
and are projected to decline at a 1.1% CAGR through 2030 to US$ 341.2 
billion. 
Despite the continued shift towards digital consumption, demand for 
in-person entertainment is increasing. Cinema, live music, out-of-home 
advertising and trade shows are expected to benefit from consumers’ 
preference for shared and immersive experiences. Global box office 
revenue is projected to grow at a 3.5% CAGR to US$ 39.5 billion by 2030, 
supported by the continued recovery of cinema. 
AI is increasingly becoming a strategic technology across the M&E 
value chain, extending beyond cost efficiencies to influence content 
creation, recommendation, discovery, personalisation, advertising and 
monetisation. Content creators can use AI tools to develop narratives and 
refine content, while platforms can use AI to better understand audience 
preferences and improve recommendations. For advertisers, AI enables 
greater precision in targeting and measurement, helping brands connect 
with consumers at relevant moments and link advertising exposure more 
closely with commercial outcomes. Connected TV and shoppable video are 
among the formats expected to benefit from this trend.
AI is also contributing to the continued shift from traditional search 
towards conversational and generative search. This is changing how 
consumers discover content and how brands approach digital visibility, 
creating greater emphasis on first-party data, content optimisation, 
influencers and AI-enabled engagement. 
Indian Media & Entertainment (M&E) Industry
India’s M&E industry continued to grow strongly in 2025 and 2026, driven 
by rapid digital adoption, rising internet penetration and shifting consumer 
preferences. According to the report ‘Stories, scale and impact: Unlocking 
India’s media and entertainment economy’ released by FICCI and EY India, 
the industry reached approximately `2.78 trillion in 2025, as compared to 
`2.56 trillion in 2024, growing 9% year-on-year.

Indian Film Industry 
The Indian film industry continued to expand in 2025, with strong growth 
in production, revenues and global reach, while also navigating shifts in 
digital and broadcast economics. In 2025, around 1,972 films (including 
dubbed versions) were released in theatres across multiple languages, up 
from 1,823 in 2024, reflecting steady growth in content creation. Despite 
this, cinema infrastructure grew only marginally, with screen count rising 
1% to about 10,033 screens.
The industry delivered its strongest box office performance to date. 
Domestic gross box office collections rose 14% year-on-year in FY 2025-
26, reaching `130 billion, while overall filmed entertainment revenues 
crossed `200 billion for the first time, growing 9% in 2025. Admissions 
also increased slightly to 868 million, but industry estimates suggest that 
fewer than 150 million unique viewers actually visited cinemas, indicating 
repeat viewership rather than broad-based penetration. However, the 
digital and broadcast segments showed some softness. Digital rights 
value declined by 8%, largely due to consolidation among OTT platforms, 
the closure of smaller regional players and tighter monetisation discipline. 
While around 500 films were available on OTT platforms, only 30 were 
direct-to-digital releases, down from 60 in 2024. Broadcast rights also 
declined by 10% as television channels continued to face pressure on 
ratings and advertising revenues.

Prime Focus Limited 60Animation, VFX (Virtual Effects) and Post-Production
The Animation, VFX and Post-Production industry plays an important role 
in the media and entertainment ecosystem by supporting films, television, 
OTT platforms, gaming, advertising and digital content creation. The 
industry combines creative talent with advanced technology to create 
animated content, visual effects, editing, colour grading, dubbing, subtitling 
and final content delivery across multiple platforms. Globally, demand for 
high-quality visual content continues to increase due to the rapid growth 
of streaming platforms, gaming and digital entertainment, creating strong 
opportunities for Indian studios and service providers.
The animation segment faced relatively softer conditions during the 
year, with revenues declining by 6% to `27 billion due to slower global 
commissioning activity, lower kids-focused advertising spends and reduced 
OTT commissioning hours. However, the segment continued to evolve as 
studios increasingly focused on IP ownership and diversified monetisation 
models combining content, commerce and distribution. Anime and young-
adult animation remained popular in India, while mythological and culturally 
rooted storytelling also gained strong audience acceptance. 
VFX remained the largest segment within the industry, reaching  `48 billion 
in 2025, driven by increasing use of visual effects and post-enhancement 
services in films and digital content. Filmmakers continued to invest 
in visually rich storytelling to enhance the viewing experience across 
theatres and premium home screens. At the same time, studios adopted 
AI-driven workflows to improve operational efficiency and manage pricing 
pressures caused by leaner production pipelines. 
The Indian animation, VFX and post-production industry showed early 
signs of recovery and stabilisation in 2025 after the slowdown witnessed 
in 2024. The overall market grew modestly by 2% to reach `105 billion. 
India continued to strengthen its position as one of the world’s largest 
content production hubs, producing nearly 200,000 hours of TV , film 
and OTT content during the year. This created steady demand for editing, 
dubbing, subtitling, localisation and other post-production services. The 
growing use of multi-language programming strategies by OTT platforms 
and broadcasters, typically across 5 to 7 languages, further supported 
demand for post-production and localisation capabilities. Rapid growth 
in short-format content and micro-dramas, with over 800 hours produced 
during the year, also contributed to industry expansion.

Industry Outlook
The outlook for the Indian Media & Entertainment industry remains 
strong, supported by rising digital adoption, higher disposable incomes 
and growing demand for premium content across formats and languages. 
The industry is expected to grow at an over-7 % CAGR between 2025 and 2028, reaching approximately `3.3 trillion by 2028, driven by digital 
media and new-age M&E segments. The filmed entertainment industry 
is expected to reach around `253 billion by 2028, driven by stronger 
theatrical revenues, wider VFX adoption, expanding screen infrastructure 
and improving international reach, while animation, VFX and post-
production are projected to grow at around 10% CAGR to approximately 
`138 billion by 2028, supported by rising OTT consumption, gaming, 
advertising, short-form content and increasing global outsourcing 
opportunities. Large-scale projects targeting global audiences, along with 
initiatives such as NFDC’s WA VES Film Bazaar, are expected to enhance 
India’s global presence across filmed entertainment, animation and VFX 
services.
AI Adoption in the M&E Industry 
AI is rapidly becoming a key growth driver for the Indian M&E industry, 
evolving from experimental use cases to practical and value-driven 
business applications. According to a survey of Indian M&E CXOs 
conducted in December 2025, nearly 60% of media companies have 
already adopted AI across content creation, processing and operational 
workflows. The technology is delivering tangible business benefits, with 
75% of respondents reporting measurable impact and 67% highlighting 
cost optimisation as a major advantage.
Content operations are emerging as one of the most promising areas 
for AI adoption, with companies increasingly using AI to improve 
automation, scalability, productivity and workflow efficiency. Media 
organisations are directing their investments toward core functions such 
as content creation, operations and distribution. At the same time, they 
are increasingly leveraging AI across the media value chain for editing, 
localisation, subtitling, metadata generation, audience analytics and 
workflow management.
Although AI investments remain selective and focused on high-impact use 
cases, the industry is steadily building stronger data capabilities, operating 
models and ROI frameworks to support wider adoption. As companies gain 
more confidence and implementation experience, AI is expected to play an 
increasingly important role in transforming content creation, distribution 
and audience engagement across the Indian M&E ecosystem.
Opportunities and Threats 
Opportunities
Digital Expansion
The global M&E industry presents significant opportunities across 
digital media, filmed entertainment, animation, VFX, gaming and regional-
language content. The continued growth of OTT platforms, connected TV , 
digital advertising, retail media and gaming is driving demand for high-
quality content and specialised media services. 
Growing OTT and Streaming Content
The continued expansion of OTT and streaming platforms is increasing 
the volume of films, series and other digital content produced globally. 
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
=== page 179 ===
Prime Focus Limited 61The shift towards ad-supported models, content bundling and multilingual 
distribution is creating opportunities across VFX, animation, post-
production, content localisation and related media services. The growing 
demand for content across multiple screens and formats also supports 
the need for scalable production and post-production capabilities.
Content Shift
Growing consumer demand for original, culturally relevant and regional 
content is expanding the addressable market for animation, VFX and 
other specialised content services. The increasing popularity of regional-
language and culturally rooted storytelling, alongside mythological, 
religious and other locally relevant content, is encouraging greater 
investment in animation, visual effects and high-quality production.
Limited Cinema Penetration
Limited access to cinema infrastructure in several emerging markets 
creates opportunities for expansion in theatrical entertainment and 
related content ecosystems. At the same time, evolving OTT release 
strategies are enabling wider and simultaneous distribution of content 
across geographies through subtitles, dubbing and localisation, creating 
additional demand for specialised media services.
Global Outsourcing
The increasing complexity and scale of global content production are 
encouraging studios, broadcasters and streaming platforms to outsource 
specialised activities such as VFX, animation and post-production. India’s 
growing relevance as a global production hub, supported by its skilled 
talent pool and competitive cost structure, creates opportunities for 
Indian media service providers to participate in international productions. 
Expanding co-production arrangements and global collaborations are 
further supporting cross-border content creation and market access.
AI-led Production
The increasing adoption of AI across the M&E value chain is creating 
opportunities to improve production efficiency, automate workflows and 
enhance content creation. AI-enabled tools can support VFX, animation, 
post-production, localisation and content processing, enabling media 
service providers to handle increasingly complex projects while improving 
productivity and turnaround times.
Live and Immersive Experiences
Growing consumer interest in live sports, concerts, cinema and immersive 
experiences is creating opportunities for high-quality visual content and 
specialised production services. 
Integrated Media Technology Solutions
The increasing convergence of content creation and technology is creating 
opportunities for companies with integrated capabilities across VFX, 
animation, post-production, localisation and media technology. Clients 
are increasingly seeking scalable, end-to-end solutions that can support 
content throughout its production and distribution lifecycle, creating opportunities for service providers to deepen client relationships and 
participate in a larger share of the value chain.
Threats
Margin Pressure
Platform consolidation across OTT and digital ecosystems is increasing 
pricing pressure and margin compression across content, animation and 
service providers. A slowdown in global commissioning and tighter scrutiny 
of ROI are also affecting outsourcing demand and animation revenues.
Cost Inflation
Rising production and operating costs, driven by technology, set, post-
production, logistics, VFX, hospitality and marketing, are impacting 
profitability. OTT-driven expectations are further increasing spend 
requirements on both production quality and promotion.
Regulatory Pressure
New Labour Codes and evolving compliance frameworks are increasing 
operational complexity across hiring, scheduling, contracting and 
budgeting. These changes are expected to raise compliance costs and 
require continuous adaptation by industry participants.

PFL has established itself as a leading independent media services and

the global entertainment ecosystem. The Company, founded in Mumbai

Prime Focus Studios operates one of India’s largest integrated production

Carter Architects in collaboration with Indian engineering teams, the studio

Section 8: Business Outlook 
The global Media & Entertainment (M&E) industry is expected to 
maintain steady growth, supported by digital consumption, advertising, 
streaming and the increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI). The 
industry is undergoing a significant transformation as AI, digital platforms 
and changing consumer preferences reshape how content is created, 
distributed and consumed. Advertising is expected to remain a key growth 
driver, while streaming, live and immersive experiences, creator-led 
content and AI-enabled production are creating new opportunities across 
the industry.  Overall, the global M&E industry is moving towards a hybrid 
model that combines digital scale with human-led experiences. The ability 
of industry participants to combine technology, data and creativity is likely 
to remain critical to capturing emerging revenue opportunities through 
2030. 
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
=== page 185 ===
Prime Focus Limited 67The Indian M&E industry is expected to remain strongly growth-oriented, 
led by rapid digital expansion across advertising and consumption 
platforms. Digital advertising is projected to contribute around `446 
billion in incremental growth by 2028, aided by rising e-commerce, point-
of-sale and SME advertising. Connected TV is also expanding from about 
40 million to nearly 67 million connections, reflecting a shift toward 
digital-first, performance-driven advertising models.
Subscription and consumption trends are similarly shifting toward digital 
ecosystems, with OTT households rising from roughly 143 million to 
about 191 million by 2028, driving `85 billion of incremental subscription 
growth. At the same time, live entertainment is expanding beyond 8 metros 
to over 20 cities with populations above 2 million, with large concert days 
rising from about 130 to over 200 by 2028, while filmed entertainment, 
animation, VFX and gaming continue to grow steadily, driven by increased 
production scale, global outsourcing and rising digital content demand.  
The Hollywood writers’ strike disrupted global entertainment supply 
chains, while international studios continued to focus on profitability in 
2025 by prioritising fewer high-value films and television projects.
Meanwhile, domestic demand strengthened as more mid-budget 
productions increasingly adopted visual effects to enhance storytelling 
and audience engagement. This created additional opportunities for 
post-production companies across emerging content segments such as advertising films, micro-dramas, adult animation and anime, which 
continued to witness growing demand.
PFL is evolving into a future-ready, technology-led content ecosystem 
positioned at the intersection of storytelling, artificial intelligence and 
immersive media. The Company is expected to continue advancing 
operational excellence while deepening global client partnerships, 
expanding end-to-end service capabilities and embedding advanced 
technologies across its workflows. Ongoing investments in innovation, 
digital infrastructure and talent are likely to strengthen its ability to scale 
sustainably in an increasingly AI-native and content-intensive world.
Looking ahead, the Company is anchored in a three-pillar architecture 
comprising DNEG (VFX & Animation), BRAHMA AI (an AI-driven enterprise 
content platform) and Prime Focus Studios (global content production 
and IP creation). DNEG is positioned to remain a core creative engine 
for next-generation filmmaking, gaming and immersive entertainment, 
accelerated by long-cycle global demand for high-end visual storytelling. 
BRAHMA AI is expected to evolve into a foundational layer for AI-powered 
content creation, localisation and workflow automation across media and 
adjacent industries, while Prime Focus Studios strengthens its role as an 
IP originator and franchise builder. Collectively, this integrated ecosystem 
positions the Company to participate in the future of content creation, 
where AI, virtual production and global storytelling converge.
Section 9: Risk Management 
The Company has a strong Risk Management framework in place to protect the business from potential internal and external risks. This framework helps 
identify, monitor, analyse and manage risks that may impact business operations. The Company also prepares and implements suitable mitigation plans 
to address different organisational risks effectively. In addition, the Company continuously monitors changes in the internal and external environment to 
identify emerging risks and take timely preventive actions.
Risk Details Mitigation Strategy
Industry Risk The Company operates in the media industry, which is con -
stantly changing due to shifting consumer preferences, chang -
ing regulations and a dynamic business environment. These 
factors can affect the Company’s profitability and long-term 
growth. Industry strikes or disruptions may also impact pro -
duction schedules, delay deliveries and reduce operational 
efficiency, which can affect brand value and business perfor -
mance.The media and entertainment industry is expected to grow 
strongly, aided by increasing digital adoption and rising 
demand for digital content.. PFL is well-positioned to manage 
industry challenges through its diversified portfolio, strong 
order book and wide global presence, helping the Company 
respond effectively to changing market conditions.
Competition Risk The media and entertainment industry offers strong growth 
opportunities, leading to intense competition from both 
domestic and international players. Rapid advancements in 
Artificial Intelligence have also made content creation and 
production processes easier and faster, increasing competitive 
pressure and creating risks for the Company’s market position.The Company follows a “world-source delivery model, ” which 
helps it deliver high-quality services within timelines. It has 
further strengthened its presence in providing premium 
services to leading Hollywood and Bollywood production 
houses. Continuous innovation, strong market initiatives and 
technological advancements help the Company maintain a 
competitive advantage. Regular engagement with studios and 
global media service providers, along with a strong focus on 
diversification and originality, enables the Company to stay 
competitive and adapt to changing industry trends.

Talent Retention 
RiskHuman resources are critical to the Company’s success. 
Business operations may be affected due to high employee 
attrition, shortage of skilled talent, overstaffing or 
understaffing, an unsuitable work environment, or industrial 
relation issues. In addition, the limited number of institutes 
offering visual effects training creates hiring challenges and 
increases the risk of losing talent to competitors.The Company follows HR policies based on industry best 
practices to create a safe, supportive and positive workplace. 
T o attract, retain and develop talented professionals, PFL 
offers competitive compensation along with training and 
development programs across all levels. The Company also 
focuses on balancing employee aspirations with organisational 
goals, helping improve employee satisfaction and retention.
Profitability Risk The media and entertainment industry operates with relatively 
low margins, which creates profitability challenges. Delays in 
the release of new content and rising costs of hiring skilled 
professionals can further increase financial pressure on the 
business.PFL has built a diversified presence across five continents, 
helping reduce dependence on any single market. The Company 
continuously invests in research and new technologies to 
improve operational efficiency and margins. Moreover, 
the company provides high quality services, enabling it to 
command industry leading margins. Its strong track record 
of delivering award-winning and commercially successful 
projects has helped it build long-term relationships with major 
production studios. In addition, the Company focuses on cost 
control measures and workforce optimisation to improve 
profitability and maintain operational efficiency.
Cyber Security Risk With increasing digitalisation, cyber security has become 
a major concern for the Company. Cyber threats such as 
data breaches, ransom ware attacks, phishing attempts 
and targeted cyber-attacks can impact the Company’s IT 
infrastructure, business operations and sensitive data.The Company has a strong IT team and follows robust cyber 
security practices across the organisation. It has implemented 
risk mitigation measures and a quick incident response 
system to handle potential cyber threats effectively. Regular 
phishing awareness campaigns are conducted to educate 
employees. The Company also regularly upgrades and backs 
up its systems, continuously improves its incident response 
plan and follows strict policies regarding the use of personal 
devices at work. PFL remains committed to strengthening its 
security framework and protecting sensitive information.

identifies and nurtures internal talent by providing training and leadership 
development opportunities to prepare future leaders. The Company aims 
to build an adaptable, future-ready workforce capable of meeting evolving 
business challenges. As of March 31, 2026, the Company and its group 
employed more than 10,200 individuals
Section 11: Internal Control and Audit 
The Company has established a strong internal control system that is 
aligned with the size of the business, the nature of its operations and the 
complexity of the industry in which it operates. PFL has implemented 
robust policies and procedures to ensure that business activities are 
conducted with integrity, transparency and accountability in a constantly 
evolving business environment. The internal control framework helps 
ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations, protects assets, 
manages risk effectively, maintains accounts accurately, prepares 
financial statements in a timely manner and detects and prevents fraud 
and errors. These controls are regularly reviewed and monitored to drive 
continuous improvement. The Company remains committed to maintaining

Prime Focus Limited 70Report on Corporate Governance
1. COMPANY’S PHILOSOPHY ON CODE OF GOVERNANCE
 The Company’s corpor ate governance philosophy rests on the pillars 
of integrity, accountability, equity, transparency and environmental 
responsibility that conform fully with laws, regulations and guidelines. 
The Company’s philosophy on corporate governance is to achieve 
business excellence and maximizing shareholder value through 
ethical business conduct. The Company’s philosophy also includes 
building partnerships with all stakeholders, employees, customers, 
vendors, service providers, local communities and government. The 
Company has always set high targets for the growth, profitability, 
customer satisfaction, safety and environmental performance and 
continues its commitment to high standards of corporate governance 
practices. During the Financial Y ear under review, the Board 
continued its pursuit of achieving its objectives through the adoption 
and monitoring of corporate strategies, prudent business plans and 
best practices in governance. By ensuring transparency, fair play and 
independence while discharging its fiduciary responsibilities, the 
Board ensures continued adherence to high standards of Corporate 
Governance.
 The Company endeavours to demonstrate the highest standards of 
Corporate Governance and ethical behaviour across the Company 
with no tolerance for any deviation from these standards. The 
Company strives to achieve long term shareholder value creation 
through responsible decision making. Being a global organisation, 
the Corporate Governance practices followed by the Company and 
its subsidiaries are compatible with international standards and 
practices.
2. BOARD OF DIRECTORS
 A diverse, independent and well informed Board functions as the 
core of any Corporate Governance philosophy. T o this end the Board 
of the Company has an optimum mix of Executive and Non-Executive 
Directors, including a woman Director.
 The Board of Directors of the Company has an appropriate mix of 
Executive Directors, Non-Executive Directors and Independent 
Directors to maintain the Board’s independence and separate its 
functions of governance and management. As on March 31, 2026, the 
Board comprises of eight (8) Directors, out of which one (1) is Whole-
time Director, three (3) are Non-Executive Non-Independent Directors 
and four (4) are Non-Executive Independent Directors including two

3. COMMITTEES OF THE BOARD
 The Board Committees plays a crucial role in the governance structure 
of the Company and have been constituted to deal with specific 
areas/activities which concern the Company and need closer review. 
The Board Committees are set up under the formal approval of the 
Board to carry out clearly defined roles. The Committees of the Board 
have oversight of specific areas delegated to them and in certain 
cases, through their recommendation facilitate decision making by 
the Board. The Board supervises the execution of responsibilities 
by the Committees and is responsible for their actions. The minutes 
of the meetings of all Committees are placed before the Board for 
review. The Board Committees can request special invitees to join the 
meeting, as appropriate.
 As on March 31, 2026, the Board has Six (6) Committees, namely Audit 
Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, Corporate 
Social Responsibility Committee, Stakeholders’ Relationship 
Committee, ESOP Compensation Committee and Risk Management 
Committee.
 The Board at its meeting held on November 12, 2025 dissolved the 
Rights Issue Committee since there was no raising of funds by way of 
Rights Issue of Equity Shares in near future.
The brief description of Committees are as follows:

of the role and capabilities required of an independent director.

• use the services of an external agencies, if required.
• consider candidates from a wide range of backgrounds, 
having due regard to diversity.
• consider the time commitments of the candidates.

(3) T o monitor and oversee implementation of the risk management 
policy, including evaluating the adequacy of risk management 
systems.
(4) T o periodically review the risk management policy, at least once 
in two years, including by considering the changing industry 
dynamics and evolving complexity.
(5) T o keep the board of directors informed about the nature and 
content of its discussions, recommendations and actions to be 
taken.
(6) The appointment, removal and terms of remuneration of the 
Chief Risk Officer (if any) shall be subject to review by the RMC.

Prime Focus Limited 81 Person who  con ducted the Postal Ballot Process
 Mr. Mehul Raval, Practicing Company Secretary, (Membership No- 
ACS 18300 and CP No- 24170) was appointed as the Scrutinizer for 
carrying out the Postal Ballot only through e-voting process for the 
above item in a fair and transparent manner. No Special Resolution is 
proposed to be conducted through Postal Ballot as on the date of this 
Report.
 Procedure for Postal Ballot
 In compliance with the Listing Regulations and Sections 108, 110 and 
other applicable provisions of the Act, read with applicable rules, the 
Company provided electronic voting facility to all its shareholders, to 
enable them to cast their votes electronically. The shareholders have 
to vote by way of remote e-voting only. The Company engaged the 
services of Central Depository Services (India) Limited ( “CDSL ” ) for 
the purpose of providing e-voting facility to all its shareholders.
 For conducting a Postal Ballot, Notice specifying the resolutions 
proposed to be passed through Postal Ballot along with Explanatory 
Statement, Instructions for e-voting, User IDs and Passwords for 
the purpose of e-voting were e-mailed to all the shareholders whose 
names appeared in register of members/ record of depositories as on 
the cut-off date i.e. Wednesday, December 31, 2025.
 The Shareholders were requested to cast their votes by e-voting using 
their User Ids and Passwords and as per the instructions mentioned in 
the Notice of Postal Ballot.
 The last date specified by the Company for remote e-voting i.e. Friday, 
February 06, 2026 was deemed to be the date of passing of the 
resolutions.
 The Scrutinizer submitted his report after the completion of scrutiny, 
and the consolidated results of the voting by remote e-voting 
were then announced by the Company Secretary. The results 
were also displayed on the website of the Company besides being 
communicated to the Stock Exchanges.

SECTION B: MANAGEMENT AND PROCESS DISCLOSURES
The National Guidelines for Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) as prescribed by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs advocates nine principles 
referred as P1-P9 as given below:
P1 Businesses should conduct and govern themselves with integrity in a manner that is ethical, transparent and accountable.
P2 Businesses should provide goods and services in a manner that is sustainable and safe.
P3 Businesses should respect and promote the well-being of all employees, including those in their value chains.
P4 Businesses should respect the interests of and be responsive towards all its stakeholders.
P5 Businesses should respect and promote human rights.
P6 Businesses should respect and make efforts to protect and restore the environment.
P7 Businesses when engaging in influencing public and regulatory policy, should do so in a manner that is responsible and transparent.
P8 Businesses should promote inclusive growth and equitable development.
P9 Businesses should engage with and provide value to their consumers in a responsible manner.

3. Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling and disposing at the end of life
 Due to the nature of our business, the potential for reusing or recycling products is limited. However, we have established specific practices to 
manage different waste categories
a) For plastics (including packaging), we use 100% biodegradable plastic garbage bags across our facilities to collect and dispose of dry and wet 
waste. At our corporate office, we partner with a vendor who disposes of our waste in an eco-friendly manner by composting or recycling.
b) Our e-waste encompasses computers, servers, scanners, Personal Computers, batteries, air conditioners, and other electronic equipment, 
which we dispose of through registered e-waste vendors.
c) We do not generate or dispose of hazardous waste in the course of our operations.
d) Aside from the waste categories listed above, we do not generate any other types of waste in our office.

 In compliance with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, the majority of our offices are accessible to differently abled employees. 
The Company is committed to provide equal opportunities without regard to their race, caste, sex, religion, color, nationality, disability, etc. All of 
our corporate offices feature such as wheelchair ramps, braille signage  and wheelchair inclusive elevators that are accessible from the parking
